Associate Editor: Jennifer Powers Handling Editor: Stephen Yanoviak

Ants are a suitable model system to analyzing morphological variation along environmental gradients because they exhibit high levels of morphological and functional variation, in addition to being extremely sensitive to environmental change (Andersen & Majer, 2004; Underwood & Fisher, 2006), especially in the tropics (Hölldobler & Wilson, 1990). During the last decade, a large and growing literature of morphological trait-based analyses on worker ants along environmental gradients has been published (e.gBihn et al., 2010; Gibb et al., 2018; Parr et al., 2017; Silva & Brandão, 2010; Yates et al., 2014) including studies linking morphological traits and ecological functions (Bihn et al., 2010; Kaspari & Weiser, 1999; Parr et al., 2017). These studies focus on average species trait values and assume that intraspecific variation is small or negligible. Thus, we still know little about morphological changes at the population level in ants. A recent study found very low levels of intraspecific variation along an elevation gradient (1–4% of total trait variation), probably masked by the large variation among species that accounted for most of the total variation (Gaudard et al., 2019). Moreover, Gibb et al. (2018) suggest that recent evolutionary pressures on ants can generate many relationships between morphological traits and the environment. Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated that workers of Leptothorax acervorum and Aphaenogaster senilis populations are larger at higher altitudes (Bernadou et al., 2016; Shik et al., 2019).

28 million people who are highly dependent on forest natural re sources for their livelihoods in a typical regime of chronic anthropogenic disturbance (Silva et al., 2017). In addition, Caatinga is highly threatened by climate change, with climate models forecasting a 22–40% reduction in rainfall and a 3–6°C increase in temperatures by 2100 (Magrin et al., 2014). Increasing aridity has been observed even within small geographic ranges (Rito et al., 2017). Thus, Caatinga offers an excellent opportunity to study potential morphological adaptations to disturbance and climate change. Moreover, previous research on the Caatinga has shown that chronic anthropogenic disturbance and/or aridity do not affect ant abundance or species richness, but does alter species composition (Arnan, Arcoverde, et al., 2018; Câmara et al., 2018; Oliveira et al., 2017) and spatial–temporal foraging activity of widely distributed species (Silva et al., 2019). Despite this, many species are unaffected and occur along a large portion of the disturbance and/or aridity gradients. Morphological traits may play an important role in how ant populations respond to increases in chronic disturbance and aridity gradients.

Our specific aims are: (1) to characterize and quantify the levels of morphological intraspecific variation within and between study plots throughout the region, (2) to verify to what extent morphological intraspecific variation depends on species or morphological trait identity, and (3) to test to what extent morphological intraspecific variation responds to changes in disturbance and aridity. We pre-dict that: (1) the degree of morphological intraspecific variation will depend on species or morphological trait identity, as previous studies have suggested that some ant clades exhibit greater trait conservatism than others (Hölldobler & Wilson, 1990; Silva & Brandão, 2010; Weiser & Kaspari, 2006), and some traits tend to be more plastic than others (Gaudard et al., 2019; Oms et al., 2017; Purcell et al., 2016; Yates et al., 2014); and (2) morphological intraspecific variation will respond to changes in disturbance and aridity, as they are the strongest environmental filters in the study area (Arnan, Arcoverde, et al., 2018; Rito et al., 2017).

We obtained water deficit/aridity data from hydrological maps of the CGIAR-CSI's Global Aridity and PET Database and Global High-Resolution Soil Water Database (Trabucco & Zomer, 2010). These maps have a 30-sec resolution, equivalent to 1 km. To plot these data onto maps, the annual average water deficit was calculated from the difference between the mean annual potential evapotranspira tion (PET) and the actual evapotranspiration (AET) using the ArcGIS 10.1 software. Water deficit ranged between 658 mm and 1086 mm.

To characterize the overall variability in ant morphology between plots along the disturbance and aridity gradients, we first used a multivariate approach, performing a principal component analysis (PCA) of ant morphological traits for each ant species. All ant morphological traits were standardized prior to the analysis. Environmental variables (aridity and disturbance) were also plotted as supplementary variables in bi-dimensional PCA space (Legendre and Legendre, 1998). We then computed the mean and

the variance for each morphological trait, species, and plot, and constructed statistical models to test the effect of disturbance and aridity on variability in ant morphology (mean and variance) for each trait and species separately. We employed Akaike's information criterion with a correction for finite sample sizes (AICc) to select the best-supported models. This approach reduces the problems associated with multiple testing, co-linearity of explanatory variables, and small sample sizes (Burnham and Anderson, 2002). Intraspecific variability within plots made the largest contribution to total variation for most morphological traits and species, but intraspecific variation between plots was considerable (Figure 1). The mean (±SE) contribution of between-plot variability to total variability was $3 7 \pm 3 \%$ (range: 16.7–85.6%) and did not differ among species $( \mathsf { A N O V A } ; F _ { 3 , 2 7 } = 0 . 2 , p = 0 . 8 6 1 )$ or morphological traits (ANOVA; $F _ { 7 , 2 3 } = 1 . 9 , p = 0 . 1 3 0 )$ . The lowest values of between-plot variability ( 70%) were for clypeus length ratio in E. muticum and D. quadriceps (Figure 1). In general, most traits were not correlated with each other, and when they were, most were not highly correlated (i.e., $r 0 . 7 0 )$ in both species. P. radoskowiskii was the ant species with fewest traits significantly correlated with each other (6 out of 28), and none of the correlation coefficients were greater than 0.70. For D. goeldii, out of the 21 possible correlation coefficients, six were significant and none of them were greater than 0.70 (Figure S3).

The contribution of between-plot variability (\~37%) to total morphological variability found here is in line with several studies on plants (Jung et al., 2010; Kazakou et al., 2014; Messier et al., 2010; Sfair et al., 2018), but differs to those reported for invertebrates, in which they display low levels of intraspecific trait variation, as found for dung beetles (3–5%, Griffiths et al., 2016) and ants (1–4%, Gaudard et al., 2019). However, while these studies analyzed a large number of species, we assessed only four ant species. Perhaps the use of the most widely distributed ant species along the gradients contributed to high between-plot intraspecific variation, as previously demonstrated for plants (Sfair et al., 2018). Species presenting a wide distribution must cope with a greater range of environmental constraints (Sanaphre-Villanueva et al., 2016; Sfair et al., 2018). Moreover, our four species may be considered generalists (Hölldobler & Wilson, 1990; Leal et al., 2017) and the similar high morphological variation shared by these species may be a mechanism that allows them to maintain populations in different environmental conditions.

Morphological trait | Measure | Function significance
Mesosoma or Weber's length | It represents body size and was measured from the base of the anterior slope of the pronotum to the lower posterior angle of the propodeum (Brown, 1953) | Strongly correlated with many physiological, ecological, and life history traits (Kaspari & Weiser, 1999)
Clypeus length ratio | Ratio of clypeus length to mesosoma length | Correlated with sucking ability and liquid-feeding behavior (Davidson et al., 2004)
Mandible length ratio | Ratio of mandible length to mesosoma length | Possible indicator of predatory lifestyle and thus types of resources consumed (Weiser & Kaspari, 2006)
Antenna length ratio | Ratio of antenna length (combined funicle and scape) to mesosoma length | Possibly correlated with ability to receive chemosensory information. Ants with long scapes may be more sensitive to pheromone trails (Weiser & Kaspari, 2006)
Leg length ratio | Ratio of leg length (combined length of femur and tibia) to mesosoma length | Possibly correlated with resource acquisition mode and foraging efficiency, as well as with the ability to cope with high foraging surface temperatures (Bihn et al., 2010; Kaspari & Weiser, 1999)
Eye length ratio | Ratio of eye length to mesosoma length | Likely correlated with main foraging period (day vs. night) (Bihn et al., 2010)
Eye position ratio | Ratio of inter-ocular width to mesosoma length | Related to hunting method (Fowler et al., 1991) or the component of the habitat occupied (Gibb & Parr, 2013)
Pilosity | Count of hairs crossing mesosoma profile | Hairs may increase tolerance to dehydration or may relate to mechanoreception (Wittlinger et al., 2007)
